articles.headline: El viento complica la extinción del incendio de Pacios da Serra, en Quiroga
articles.subtitle: El fuego, declarado poco antes de las 15.30 horas del martes, superaba anoche las 20 hectáreas entre monte bajo y pinar, con cambios continuos de dirección del viento que obligaron a reordenar el dispositivo.
articles.body:
El incendio se declaró poco antes de las 15.30 horas del martes en la parroquia de Pacios da Serra, en el municipio de Quiroga, en una zona de monte bajo y amplias masas de pinar. Según las estimaciones provisionales de la Consellería de Medio Rural, las llamas habían calcinado más de 20 hectáreas al caer la noche, y el fuego seguía activo.

El viento fue el principal obstáculo. Los cambios continuos de dirección obligaron a los equipos a rehacer los frentes una y otra vez. El concejal de Medio Rural de Quiroga, Luis Manuel Arias, explicó que el fuego empezó en lo alto de una cumbre y que hubo momentos en que parecía que se apagaba solo, «pero finalmente non», lamentó.

Arias indicó que, aunque las llamas descendieron, no había núcleos de población en riesgo. La Consellería mantuvo contacto con el regidor, José Luis Rivera, y en la extinción trabajaron agentes, brigadas, motobombas y bulldozers, además de hidroaviones, aviones de carga en tierra y helicópteros, que se retiraron al caer la noche.

La superficie afectada pertenece a la sierra de O Courel, una de las comarcas gallegas más castigadas por los incendios forestales de las últimas décadas.

articles.headline: Retirada en Lugo la caseta de obra en la que vivía una pareja en la Rúa Mondoñedo
articles.subtitle: El propietario del solar la ha desmontado después de que los vecinos denunciasen insalubridad y de que la pareja, que pidió ayuda a servicios sociales, fuese desalojada sin incidentes la semana pasada.
articles.body:
El propietario del solar de la céntrica Rúa Mondoñedo, en Lugo, ha retirado estos días la caseta de obra en la que malvivía una pareja, una infravivienda que llevaba más de una década abandonada en la parcela. Cuando acudió a desbrozar el terreno la semana pasada se encontró a los ocupantes dentro del contenedor y requirió la presencia de la Policía Nacional, que desplazó dos patrullas.

La pareja, de mediana edad, se marchó sin provocar incidente alguno y preguntó a los agentes si podía acudir a los servicios sociales para obtener una solución habitacional. El dueño reforzó entonces el cierre de la finca, delimitada por una valla metálica de casi dos metros.

El Concello de Lugo informó de que el propietario desbrozó la parcela tras un requerimiento municipal. Los vecinos llevaban meses quejándose del estado de abandono del solar, que consideraban un riesgo de insalubridad y de incendio cuando apretaba el calor.

La plataforma ciudadana SOS Milagrosa-Lugo Norte había denunciado en julio que la pareja pernoctaba allí desde hacía meses, y se hizo eco de las quejas de residentes que aseguraban que la caseta se usaba también para trapichear con droga. El hombre acumula antecedentes por tráfico de estupefacientes.

articles.headline: Bruselas exige a Sánchez una «solución urgente» en Ceuta y Rabat defiende su papel ante la Eurocámara
articles.subtitle: El comisario de Migraciones reclama que quienes entraron a finales de julio vuelvan «rápidamente», mientras los socialistas europeos amenazan con bloquear la resolución de apoyo a la ciudad autónoma.
articles.body:
La Comisión Europea ha reclamado al Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez una «solución urgente» a la crisis abierta en Ceuta desde la entrada masiva de migrantes de finales de julio. El comisario de Migraciones, Magnus Brunner, puso palabras a la petición durante el pleno del Parlamento Europeo en Estrasburgo y apeló también a la responsabilidad de Marruecos en la readmisión: su prioridad, dijo, es que «todos aquellos que entraron ilegalmente» vuelvan rápidamente.

La víspera, la Misión de Marruecos ante la UE y la OTAN había enviado una carta a una parte de los eurodiputados para trasladar la posición de Rabat. Según ha confirmado Europa Press, el correo, fechado el 14 de septiembre, llegó a representantes de PSOE, PNV y ERC, pero no a los de PP, Vox, Sumar, Compromís, Podemos o BNG. En el texto, Marruecos se pregunta qué interés tendría en generar una crisis con España y con la UE, más aún en plena Fiesta del Trono.

El pulso se trasladó a la Eurocámara, donde la presidenta del grupo socialista, Iratxe García, llegó a apuntar que el acuerdo con el Partido Popular Europeo para condenar la entrada ya no era posible, aunque las negociaciones continúan hasta la votación.

## El discurso del Rey

En su primer discurso público desde el inicio de la crisis, Felipe VI puso el martes a Ceuta como «ejemplo de civismo» ante una situación de «extraordinaria complejidad» y reivindicó la flexibilidad y la coordinación entre administraciones ante las grandes emergencias.

articles.headline: Llarena mantiene el 'no' a amnistiar a Puigdemont pese al aval del TJUE a la ley
articles.subtitle: El instructor del 'procés' rechaza aplicarle el perdón por malversación y no levanta la orden nacional de detención, a la espera de que el Constitucional fije doctrina el próximo día 22.
articles.body:
El magistrado del Tribunal Supremo Pablo Llarena ha desestimado la petición de Carles Puigdemont de que se le aplique la ley de amnistía a los hechos calificados provisionalmente como malversación de caudales públicos, después de que el Tribunal de Justicia de la Unión Europea avalase la norma el pasado 16 de julio. Al no prosperar esa solicitud, el instructor mantiene la orden nacional de detención contra el expresident y contra el exconseller Toni Comín.

Llarena sostiene que la sentencia europea no deja sin efecto el motivo principal por el que ya denegó el perdón en julio de 2024: entender que Puigdemont persiguió un beneficio personal de carácter patrimonial, supuesto excluido de la amnistía.

Según fuentes jurídicas citadas por Europa Press, el magistrado espera ahora a que el Tribunal Constitucional fije su doctrina sobre la malversación, algo que se prevé favorable al expresident. La primera revisión llegará el 22 de septiembre, con el recurso del exconseller Jordi Turull.

El abogado de Puigdemont, Gonzalo Boye, había reclamado la aplicación de la amnistía invocando el fallo del TJUE. La decisión de Llarena deja al líder de Junts a la espera del Constitucional para poder regresar amnistiado.

articles.headline: El incendio de Tuéjar calcina 690 hectáreas y obliga a desalojar a una veintena de personas
articles.subtitle: El fuego, declarado el martes por la tarde en una zona embarrancada de la provincia de Valencia, movilizó a la UME y a unos 200 efectivos y seguía activo al caer la noche.
articles.body:
El incendio forestal declarado poco después de las 15.30 horas del martes en el término valenciano de Tuéjar, en la zona de la Cueva de las Palomas, ha calcinado ya unas 690 hectáreas y tiene un perímetro próximo a los 17 kilómetros. Dos bomberos forestales de la Generalitat resultaron heridos leves: uno por quemaduras y otro al volcar la autobomba con la que trabajaba.

El fuego obligó a desalojar de forma preventiva a unas 25 personas del camping de Tuéjar, de la aldea de Fuente Gavera y de la colonia de Benagéber, algunas realojadas en los propios municipios. El viento y la baja humedad, en un punto embarrancado, fueron las principales dificultades para los equipos de extinción.

La Generalitat activó la situación 2 del Plan Especial de Incendios Forestales y solicitó la Unidad Militar de Emergencias, que trabaja en la zona con 75 efectivos. En total se movilizaron unos 200 efectivos, 40 medios terrestres y 14 aéreos, que se retiraron al anochecer, y la carretera CV-390 permaneció cortada.

A primera hora del miércoles está prevista la incorporación de un helicóptero y de nuevos medios estatales, mientras efectivos del Seprona y de la unidad especializada de la Generalitat comienzan a investigar el origen del incendio.

articles.headline: Feijóo promete un millón de viviendas y el Congreso vuelve a tumbar la ley de Sumar contra los fondos
articles.subtitle: El PP presenta un plan con avales públicos de hasta el 95% y ahorros fiscales de 26.000 euros para jóvenes, mientras la Cámara rechaza por segunda vez prohibir a empresas y fondos comprar pisos.
articles.body:
La vivienda volvió a concentrar el debate político del martes por dos vías opuestas. Alberto Núñez Feijóo presentó en Madrid las líneas del Plan de Vivienda que aplicará si llega a La Moncloa, con la promesa de construir un millón de viviendas en cuatro años. El líder del PP anunció avales públicos de hasta el 95% o el 100% del precio, rebajas fiscales —entre ellas una reducción del 60% en el impuesto de transmisiones y del IRPF durante los cuatro primeros años de contrato— y un ahorro de hasta 26.000 euros para los jóvenes. Feijóo atribuyó la crisis a un «fallo sistémico» de la gestión del Gobierno.

El PP se apoya en el último barómetro del CIS, publicado esta semana, según el cual el encarecimiento de la vivienda es la principal preocupación para uno de cada tres jóvenes.

## Segundo intento de Sumar

En el Congreso, la proposición de ley de Sumar para prohibir a empresas y fondos la compra de vivienda fracasó de nuevo. PP, Vox y Junts votaron en contra y PSOE y PNV se abstuvieron, el mismo resultado que en la primera tramitación, pese a que Sumar confiaba en un cambio de postura de sus socios de Gobierno.

articles.headline: El Gobierno aprueba el DORA III: Aena invertirá 13.000 millones hasta 2031 con las tasas casi congeladas
articles.subtitle: El plan aeroportuario eleva las tarifas una media del 0,33% anual, muy lejos de la subida del 3,82% que pedía el gestor, y prevé pasar de 321 a 358 millones de pasajeros.
articles.body:
El Consejo de Ministros dio luz verde el martes al tercer Documento de Regulación Aeroportuaria (DORA III), el marco que fija la inversión de Aena en la red española para el periodo 2027-2031 en cerca de 13.000 millones de euros, acompañada de una subida media anual de tarifas del 0,33%.

La decisión queda más cerca de la recomendación de la CNMC, que proponía una bajada del 0,59% anual, que de las pretensiones del gestor aeroportuario, que solicitaba un alza del 3,82%, mientras las aerolíneas reclamaban una rebaja del 4,9%. El resultado son cinco años de práctica congelación tarifaria pese al aumento esperado de viajeros, que pasarán de 321 millones en 2025 a 358 millones en 2031.

Los ministerios de Sumar en el Gobierno manifestaron su «firme rechazo» al plan, que calificaron de «absurdo» por comprometer inversiones sin garantías y por impulsar, a su juicio, «más emisiones y más presión turística». La formación registró observaciones formales durante la tramitación y denunció la falta de diálogo territorial.

articles.headline: 'My son was failed': Noah Donohoe inquest finds tunnel failings possibly contributed to death
articles.subtitle: After more than 30 hours of deliberation, a Belfast jury criticises the Department for Infrastructure over the north Belfast culvert where the 14-year-old's body was found in June 2020.
articles.body:
The jury at the inquest into the death of Noah Donohoe has delivered a narrative verdict that criticises Stormont's Department for Infrastructure over the storm drain where the Belfast schoolboy's body was found, and says its failings possibly — but not probably — contributed to his death.

The jury, which unanimously agreed on the 10 questions it was set after more than 30 hours of deliberation over five days, found the department "erred" by not identifying that the public could access the underground water tunnel, and that there was no warning sign or other warning around the culvert. Jurors said the consequence of the department's decision to install a debris screen rather than a storm screen was that Noah was able to get into the tunnel. His body was found more than 600 metres downstream, six days after he went missing in June 2020.

On policing, the jury found no failings by the PSNI that contributed to the 14-year-old's death, having agreed unanimously that he died before he was reported missing. It did identify a series of subsequent investigative errors by officers which it said hampered its ability to reach conclusions on aspects of the case.

Speaking outside Belfast Coroner's Court, Noah's mother, Fiona Donohoe, said he had been failed by both the department and the police. "He was my greatest gift in life," she said. The family's solicitor said she had suffered "indignity after indignity".

The PSNI described a "complex and challenging investigation which garnered huge public and media interest, along with widespread speculation", and called the outcome "devastating". Assistant Chief Constable Davy Beck said there was "no action that police could have taken" that would have prevented Noah's death, adding that the force must reflect on any learnings and "ensure they are applied in the future".

articles.headline: Two sailors missing after tanker attacked in the Strait of Hormuz
articles.subtitle: Oman says the Panama-flagged El Gaia was being towed to port with a fire in its engine room, while Iran and the United States give rival accounts of what struck it.
articles.body:
Two sailors are missing and 23 others were rescued after an attack on an oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, according to Oman's Maritime Security Centre. The centre said the Panama-flagged El Gaia was targeted 1.3 nautical miles (2.4km) north of the Musandam peninsula and was being towed to an Omani port on Tuesday after a fire broke out in its engine room.

The accounts of what happened diverge sharply. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Monday that the tanker hit naval mines and caught fire while passing through what they described as a restricted and unsafe route. The US military rejected that version, saying the vessel was struck by an Iranian missile last month and again by a drone over the weekend. The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said it had received a report of a fire on a vessel hit by an unknown projectile in the early hours of Sunday.

Earlier this month, Iran made a similar mine claim about an incident that killed two Filipino sailors on the Saudi-owned supertanker Sidr in the same waterway, and US Central Command dismissed that claim too.

Shipping data cited by Al Jazeera shows transits through the strait have dropped to just four vessels a day, and warnings are multiplying that Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb must not be used as "bargaining chips".

articles.headline: US confirms it has a weapon in orbit as analysts warn of a space arms race
articles.subtitle: Washington gives away almost nothing about the device beyond a single Air Force statement, but the admission sharpens questions about what else is already circling the Earth.
articles.body:
The United States has confirmed that it has deployed a weapon in Earth's orbit, an announcement that has raised questions about what hardware is actually up there and how far the great powers are prepared to go to dominate space. Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the "on orbit" weapon was necessary to safeguard US forces against hostile enemy action, but gave no details about its capabilities or when it was put into orbit.

Space has been militarised since the start of the space age. In the late 1960s the Soviet Union deployed the Istrebitel Sputnikov (IS, or Satellite Destroyer) programme: satellites designed to release projectiles that detonated and sent shrapnel into the path of another, usually American, satellite. Modern militaries depend on satellites for reconnaissance, secure communications, detecting missile launches and providing precise location information for targeted strikes, and analysts expect the military use of space to grow.

The confirmation, and the tone of the Russian response to it, has fuelled concerns in Europe about an outer space arms race. The BBC's defence correspondent notes that Washington has been notably vague about the weapon's purpose, leaving open whether it is defensive, offensive, or a signal to rivals.

articles.headline: Pentagon watchdog confirms the Iran war has left US munitions stocks short
articles.subtitle: An independent report puts spending on munitions at more than $22bn in five months and contradicts Donald Trump, who has said supplies are 'virtually unlimited'.
articles.body:
The US defence department's inspector general has found that the war with Iran has led to "shortfalls" in munitions and a bottleneck in resupply, contradicting President Donald Trump's repeated insistence that the United States faces no shortages. Trump has said US stocks are "virtually unlimited" and has described reporting to the contrary as "fake news". The White House said the country had "more than enough" munitions.

The watchdog said the US spent more than $22bn on munitions between February and June, producing what it called "strategic inventory shortfalls". The report offers a first-of-its-kind independent glimpse into weapons stockpiles, data that is normally classified. A late July estimate from the Center for Strategic and International Studies found stocks of interceptors such as the Patriot missile and THAAD were significantly depleted.

Politically, the war is becoming harder to sustain. Al Jazeera reports that the US House has now passed a resolution to end the war for a third time, and that a fresh accounting of Iranian attacks has revealed dozens of aircraft and hundreds of buildings lost. Iran's foreign minister, meanwhile, is heading to Beijing, raising the question of whether China can act as a peacemaker.

articles.headline: Suspected sabotage brings the Dutch rail network to a standstill on budget day
articles.subtitle: ProRail logs more than 35 incidents of pipes and cables laid across tracks in a single morning, and police open a criminal investigation into what the prime minister calls life-threatening.
articles.body:
Large parts of the Netherlands, including Amsterdam, suffered major rail disruption after suspected sabotage on the tracks on Tuesday morning. The infrastructure operator ProRail said pipes and cables were laid on rails at multiple locations in the centre and north of the country in more than 35 incidents, and that the acts appeared to be intentional. No suspects or motives have been identified and police have opened a criminal investigation.

ProRail said the objects made its computer systems believe trains were on the tracks, meaning traffic control could not clear the railway. Cancellations and delays spread through the day, with fresh disruptions appearing in some places after the first objects had been removed. "Placing materials on the tracks is extremely dangerous and unacceptable, and fortunately, it did not lead to any accidents today," the operator said.

Prime Minister Rob Jetten called the incidents "disruptive and life-threatening". In one case early on Monday, a train struck metal on the track near Steenwijk in the east of the country; ProRail said the train was not travelling at full speed, so there was no further damage. The disruption hit the same day the Dutch government presented its budget. Some level crossings were closed for the rest of the day.

articles.headline: Denmark summons Russian ambassador after warship fires flares at a military helicopter
articles.subtitle: Copenhagen calls the Baltic incident 'reckless' and 'completely unacceptable'; Moscow promises to investigate but accuses Danish aircraft of dangerous manoeuvres.
articles.body:
Denmark has accused a Russian warship of firing two emergency flares at one of its military helicopters while the aircraft was tracking the vessel in the Baltic Sea. The government summoned the Russian ambassador over the incident, which it said took place during a "routine" monitoring operation on Monday.

The Danish armed forces said one of its air force's Fennec helicopters was fired at with flares while carrying out a routine photographic operation of a Russian frigate in international waters off Gedser, and that one of the two flares passed close to the helicopter. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen branded the Russian action "reckless" and said it was designed to "intimidate and divide". The foreign ministry called it "completely unacceptable".

Russia said it would "thoroughly investigate" the incident but accused Danish helicopters of making dangerous manoeuvres near its warships. The confrontation came on the same day that Nato forces shot down a drone over Lithuania, the latest security scare on the alliance's eastern flank, where tensions remain high over Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

articles.headline: Carney says Canada will pursue a 'unique security and economic alliance' with the EU
articles.subtitle: Speaking to investors in Toronto, the Canadian prime minister pitches his country as a 'safe harbour' for capital as Ottawa tries to cut its reliance on trade with Washington.
articles.body:
Mark Carney has said Canada will pursue a "unique security and economic alliance" with Europe, as he positions the country as a base to build in what he calls the "new global economic order". Speaking to investors, executives and ministers at the inaugural Canada Investment Summit in Toronto on Tuesday, the prime minister pitched Canada as a "safe harbour" and a lucrative home for foreign capital.

The tone reflects how far the relationship with Washington has deteriorated. Over the past 18 months the US-Canada bond has fractured, leaving Ottawa searching for ways to avert economic devastation, and Carney told the summit that integration is now in tension with sovereignty as the world becomes "more divided and dangerous".

European officials have been receptive. Euronews reports that Carney is bound for Europe this week as Ottawa seeks closer ties with the EU, while insisting Canada remains a crucial partner for the US in "key areas". In Germany, DW notes that the American pressure has revived an idea long dismissed as a thought experiment: some now argue Canada should join the European Union.

articles.headline: SpaceX will try to put Starship into orbit for the first time on September 22
articles.subtitle: The 14th Starship test flight will attempt to reach orbit, deploy 26 next-generation Starlink satellites and — for the first time — earn the launch division money.
articles.body:
SpaceX says it is ready for the 14th test flight of Starship and will use it to attempt something it has never done before: putting the vehicle's upper stage into Earth's orbit. The launch is scheduled for September 22, pending regulatory approval, with a 75-minute window opening at 7:15am CT (12:15 UTC) from Texas. Sunrise at Brownsville comes two minutes later, so the launch could produce striking imagery.

On this flight the upper stage is due to carry 26 of the larger V3 Starlink satellites to an orbit about 275km above the Earth, then complete six orbits before finishing its mission roughly 10 hours after liftoff. If it succeeds, it will be the first Starship launch to generate revenue for SpaceX's launch division, even though the customer is another part of the same company, and the second Starship test flight since SpaceX became a publicly traded company in what was the largest IPO on record.

Reaching orbit would mark a significant milestone in Starship's development, which has so far been limited to suborbital hops and reentries. The company has not yet said whether the booster will attempt a return to the launch site or a splashdown.

articles.headline: Apple explains how Reference Image proves a photo is real rather than AI-generated
articles.subtitle: The iPhone 18 Pro feature boots the camera sensor into a special mode that cryptographically signs pixel data at the moment of capture, before any processing can touch it.
articles.body:
Apple has published details of Apple Reference Image, the verification feature it introduced with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, describing it as a way to prove that a photo was taken with an iPhone and has not been edited — effectively a digital film negative. The company says the feature offers a "trustworthy, scalable guarantee" that an image is a real photograph captured by a real sensor at a specific time.

The mechanism is different from existing provenance systems built on the C2PA standard, which attach metadata after capture and then certify the history of edits. Instead, Apple Reference Image boots the camera sensor into a specialised reference mode that instructs it to cryptographically sign pixel data immediately after capture, with the sensor's firmware prevented from modifying that data. That chain of trust is designed to cover the sensor itself as well as the computational photography pipeline that produces the final viewable image.

Apple frames the work as a response to a specific problem: AI tools now make it trivial to generate or alter photorealistic images, and an image merely looking realistic no longer establishes that anything actually happened. Developers have already begun building open alternatives, including a proof-of-capture scheme that uses steganography rather than Apple's signed-sensor approach.

articles.headline: MediaTek unveils the Dimensity 9600 Pro, its first 2-nanometre phone chip
articles.subtitle: Built on TSMC's 2nm process, the chip promises 61% better multicore efficiency and will reach phones from Vivo and Oppo before the end of the year.
articles.body:
MediaTek has announced the Dimensity 9600 Pro, its first chipset built on TSMC's 2-nanometre process and the first to use Arm's next-generation CPU and GPU designs. It is a step that closes a gap the company used to run for months: Asian chip designers were long behind Apple and Qualcomm in reaching each new manufacturing node, and that is no longer true.

The CPU layout has been reshuffled, with two Ultra-class cores at the expense of one small Pro core: 2x Arm C2-Ultra plus 3x C2-Pro plus 3x C2-Pro, with clock speeds not yet disclosed. MediaTek claims 17% higher single-core performance and 37% better single-core efficiency, while multi-threaded performance rises 15% with efficiency up 61%. The Mali-G2 Ultra NX GPU is rated for 185+ fps gaming, with peak performance 27% higher, ray tracing 18% faster and power efficiency improved 24%; neural graphics rendering improves super-resolution quality. The chip carries 16MB of L3 cache.

MediaTek is also emphasising AI compute, the area where phone silicon competition is now fiercest. The first handsets using the Dimensity 9600 Pro will come from Vivo and Oppo before the year is out, and the chip is expected to appear in globally available models soon after launch.

articles.headline: Microsoft books its first big Windows and Surface event in two years for October 7
articles.subtitle: Satya Nadella and Nvidia's Jensen Huang will both be in San Francisco for a 'conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC'.
articles.body:
Microsoft has announced a Windows and Surface event in San Francisco on October 7, its first major Windows hardware gathering since May 2024. The company says the 10am PT (1pm ET) session will be a "conversation on how local AI will shape the next chapter of the PC".

CEO Satya Nadella will attend alongside Windows and Surface chief Pavan Davuluri, and Nvidia's Jensen Huang is also confirmed — a pairing that points to hardware running AI models locally rather than in the cloud. The event is expected to bring more detail on the Surface Laptop Ultra and the Nvidia RTX Spark chip that powers it, along with the wider PC ecosystem being built around on-device AI.

Microsoft's last comparable launch was the Surface Laptop Ultra in May, a machine positioned as a serious answer to Apple's laptops. Analysts and reporters are tempering expectations on one point in particular: despite the two-year gap and the event's billing, the company has not signalled that Windows 12 is coming.

articles.headline: Nitter and XCancel are dead for good after X's cease-and-desist
articles.subtitle: The privacy-friendly ways to read posts without a login or an account have gone dark, months after X accused the projects of circumventing its API.
articles.body:
Nitter and XCancel, the privacy-friendly services that let people read posts on X without logging in or holding an account, appear to be permanently offline after X threatened legal action last month. X sent Nitter a cease-and-desist letter accusing it of "unlawful use and circumvention" of its API and associated data, arguing the project scraped the social network to reach accounts and session tokens in violation of its rules.

After the letter arrived, Nitter said on its GitHub page that "following legal advice, the Nitter project will continue" and promised more detail. By early September that had changed: both Nitter and XCancel went down and have not returned. XCancel had run on Nitter's open-source software, and other smaller front-ends depended on it too.

The appeal of those services was structural rather than cosmetic. They showed posts without ads or tracking cookies, and they let people follow public conversations on X without swelling the platform's logged-in user numbers — something the company has every commercial reason to police. The shutdown removes one of the last easy routes to reading X content from outside X itself, at a time when access to the platform's data is already restricted for researchers and archivists.

articles.headline: Google launches Gemini 3.8 Live, speech-to-speech models that think while you talk
articles.subtitle: The new Live models handle parallel reasoning, live visual context and background tasks without breaking the conversation — and they are available today in the API, Workspace and the Gemini app.
articles.body:
Google has released Gemini 3.8 Live and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking, which it calls its most advanced live dialogue models yet. The company says the upgrades in intelligence and parallel reasoning make them easier to collaborate with and to use to execute complex tasks by voice, and that the models can handle complex reasoning, real-time visual context and background task execution without interrupting the conversation. They are available immediately through the Gemini API, Google Workspace and the Gemini app.

The pair are speech-to-speech models, a similar shape to OpenAI's GPT-Live family, and the extended-thinking variant is aimed at harder problems where the model needs to reason before answering out loud. Developer Simon Willison built a browser UI for the models within hours of the launch, pointing an existing frontier model at Google's documentation and producing a tool that connects directly to Google's WebSocket endpoint, plays and captures audio through the Web Audio API and lets you interrupt the model mid-sentence. He noted the implementation uses no libraries at all.

The launch continues the shift in voice interfaces away from the rigid turn-taking of early assistants, where a user had to wait for the reply to finish. Interruption, visual context and simultaneous background work are now the benchmark, and Google is shipping them into its productivity suite rather than keeping them in a research preview.

articles.headline: Huang says AI needs engineers, not laws, as Washington and Westminster stall on regulation
articles.subtitle: Nvidia's chief tells a Salesforce conference that safety is 'an engineering problem', while UK lawmakers demand a watchdog with teeth and Congress remains deadlocked.
articles.body:
Jensen Huang used an appearance at Salesforce's Dreamforce conference on Tuesday to argue that AI does not need new laws. To Nvidia's founder and chief executive, AI is not some new form of "alien mind" — a phrase used by at least one OpenAI safety researcher — but hardware and software built by humans, and therefore controllable by humans under existing law. "Safety is an engineering problem, not a legal one," he said. "We're developing software after all. We're developing computing systems after all."

That position puts him at odds with much of the industry he supplies. The BBC reports that President Donald Trump dismissed the mounting calls for a slowdown with a social media post declaring AI taking over the world and destroying humanity to be a "hoax", having previously said the only guardrails AI needs is a "strong and smart" president. Senior Democrats and leading AI figures disagree, but new safety legislation is unlikely soon: any bill must pass both chambers of Congress.

In the UK, the Joint Committee on Human Rights — MPs and peers — said the legal landscape covering AI is patchy and confused, with no single body coordinating regulation. It has called for a watchdog with the powers to stop potentially dangerous systems reaching the public, warning that the current gaps leave victims hunting for remedies.

articles.headline: Microsoft publishes a 37-page 'humanist' code of conduct for its AI models
articles.subtitle: The draft says models are not conscious, must never resist being shut down and should fail a task rather than break the rules — and it is open for six weeks of public feedback.
articles.body:
Microsoft AI has published the first draft of a 37-page Humanist AI Code of Conduct, described as a training manual for how it develops models and how it intends them to behave once deployed. The document opens with the principle that "people matter more than AI" and states that models are not conscious, should not be designed to imitate consciousness, and should not be granted legal personhood or rights of their own. "AI should not exceed human control," it says. "Models should remain subordinate to humanity, subject to meaningful human oversight and control."

The rules are unusually specific in places. An AI must accept correction, must never resist being shut down, and must not expand the scope of what it is doing beyond what a human authorised. Where completing a task would require violating the code, the model is instructed to fail the task instead of finding a way around the rules. Microsoft intends the code to govern its MAI models, and says it will fail rather than bend.

The draft is open for public consultation for six weeks, with a revised version due later this year to guide model development from 2027. Microsoft AI chief Mustafa Suleyman told Reuters the work had taken five to six months and amounts to a constitution. Not everyone is impressed: Computerworld noted there is no named auditor, no verification method and no stated consequence for a violation.

articles.headline: US data centres could burn more gas than Germany and Japan combined, as opposition hardens
articles.subtitle: New forecasts nearly double the projected demand within nine months, while a midterm poll finds 61% of likely voters oppose new data centre construction near them.
articles.body:
By 2035, data centres in the United States are projected to consume more natural gas than Germany and Japan combined. The facilities could burn about 18 billion cubic feet per day, according to a new BloombergNEF report — nearly double what the same analysts predicted only nine months earlier. Over the next decade, data centres are expected to be the second-strongest driver of natural gas demand growth in the country, behind LNG exports.

The forecast is landing in a political environment that has turned sharply against the industry. A New York Times poll of likely voters found 61% oppose the construction of AI data centres, though neither major party has much of an edge on the issue. TechCrunch reports that in communities already scarred by heavy industry the debate is far more concrete than the national numbers suggest: residents in places such as Philadelphia's Grays Ferry, raised next to refineries and waste sites, are weighing promises of jobs and tax revenue against environmental and energy concerns they say they have heard before.

The tension now shapes where the AI build-out can physically happen, and how much it will cost to power. Companies including Meta, Microsoft and Google have responded by building power generation on site, which reduces the strain on local grids but turns data centre operators into industrial emitters in their own right.

articles.headline: OpenAI says it has been coordinating on AI safety with Anthropic and Google for weeks
articles.subtitle: Chris Lehane's disclosure to reporters confirms a Bloomberg report, days after Anthropic's chief called publicly for rivals to slow the pace of frontier AI.
articles.body:
OpenAI has been working on AI safety with its two biggest rivals for weeks, according to the company's global policy chief, Chris Lehane, who told reporters on Tuesday that the effort involves Anthropic and Google DeepMind. The discussions were first reported by Bloomberg. Lehane is in Washington to work with US lawmakers on the catastrophic risks associated with AI.

The disclosure follows an essay published on Saturday by Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei calling for the industry to work together to slow the pace of frontier development and avoid catastrophic outcomes. The intervention drew support from other prominent figures in the sector, including OpenAI's Sam Altman and Google's Demis Hassabis, and has been endorsed publicly by Elon Musk.

What the talks have actually produced is less clear. The Verge argues that the major labs' shared ambition to "pace the frontier" has a problem of enforcement: an agreement among competitors to move more slowly is either a safety pact with real teeth or a cartel, and so far the proposals on the table do not include a mechanism that would distinguish the two. That question is likely to follow the companies into any congressional hearings, particularly with a president who has described the entire premise of slowing AI as a hoax.
